passages.t: Terrible times: lovers of self, money and pleasure
passages.happening:
“But understand this: In the last days terrible times will come” (verse 1).

Then Paul gives a long list of what people will be like. “For men will be lovers of themselves, lovers of money, boastful, arrogant, abusive, disobedient to their parents, ungrateful, unholy, unloving, unforgiving, slanderous, without self-control, brutal, without love of good, traitorous, reckless, conceited, lovers of pleasure rather than lovers of God, having a form of godliness but denying its power. Turn away from such as these!” (verses 2-5).
passages.hearers:
‘The last days’ sounds as if Paul means some time far in the future. But in the New Testament the last days began when Christ came. Peter said so on the day of Pentecost (Acts 2:17), and Hebrews says God has spoken to us ‘in these last days’ by his Son (Hebrews 1:2). The last days are the whole time between Christ's first coming and his return. That is why Paul tells Timothy to turn away from such people now. They were already in the church at Ephesus.

Look at how the list begins and ends. It starts with ‘lovers of themselves’ and ‘lovers of money’. It ends with ‘lovers of pleasure rather than lovers of God’. Everything in between grows from love pointed the wrong way. When people love themselves, money and pleasure in the place of God, all the rest follows: pride, cruelty, broken families, betrayal.

The last line is the sharpest. These people have ‘a form of godliness’. The word means an outward shape. They look religious. They may go to worship and use the right words. But they deny the power of godliness, the power of God that changes a life. The outside is there, and the inside is empty.

Notice who Paul is talking about. Not the pagan city outside. People inside the church, who kept the look of faith without its life.
passages.ot:
The great command was to love God first: “And you shall love the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your strength” (Deuteronomy 6:5). The list in verses 2-4 is that command turned upside down.

The prophets knew the danger of religion that was only on the outside. “These people draw near to Me with their mouths and honor Me with their lips, but their hearts are far from Me” (Isaiah 29:13). Jeremiah warned people who trusted in the temple building but not in God: “Do not trust in deceptive words” (Jeremiah 7:4). And Micah said what God really asks: “to act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God” (Micah 6:8).
passages.hard:
Does ‘in the last days’ mean that we can tell how near the end is, or name the people Paul describes?

No. In the New Testament the last days are the whole time between Christ's first coming and his return, and Paul was describing people already troubling the church in Timothy's day. Every generation since has had people like this, and every generation has been tempted to say, ‘This is it. The end is here.’ But Jesus said, “No one knows about that day or hour” (Mark 13:32). This passage gives no date, and it does not point to any group of people today.

It is also easy to read this list as a description of other people: the culture, the other party, the young, the world out there. That turns the passage around. Paul is warning about people inside the church who looked godly. The list is a mirror before it is a window. ‘Lovers of themselves’, ‘lovers of money’, ‘a form of godliness but denying its power’: any of us can become these things, and the first place to look is our own heart.
passages.asks: Paul's list grows from love pointed the wrong way. Ask what you love most, honestly: yourself, money, pleasure, or God. Ask whether your faith has the look of godliness without its power, words without a changed life. And before you think of anyone else who fits this list, ask where you fit it.

passages.t: Deceivers in households, like Jannes and Jambres
passages.happening:
Paul describes how the false teachers work. “They are the kind who worm their way into households and captivate vulnerable women who are weighed down with sins and led astray by various passions, who are always learning but never able to come to a knowledge of the truth” (verses 6-7).

“Just as Jannes and Jambres opposed Moses, so also these men oppose the truth. They are depraved in mind and disqualified from the faith. But they will not advance much further. For just like Jannes and Jambres, their folly will be plain to everyone” (verses 8-9).
passages.hearers:
The church met in homes. There were no church buildings. So a false teacher could gain a hearing by visiting houses, perhaps while the men were away at work. Paul says these teachers ‘worm their way’ in, a phrase for slipping in where you have no right to be.

He describes the people they had won over in Ephesus: certain women who were ‘vulnerable’, ‘weighed down with sins’, pulled about by their desires, always taking in new teaching but never arriving at the truth. These were particular people, in a particular city, whom the false teachers had found and used. Paul's anger is at the teachers who preyed on them.

Jannes and Jambres are not named in the Old Testament. Exodus speaks only of Pharaoh's magicians, who copied the signs Moses did. But Jewish tradition gave those magicians names, and these are the names Paul's readers knew. His point is simple. The magicians could copy Moses for a while, and then they could not. Aaron's staff swallowed theirs (Exodus 7:12), and soon they could not copy God's work at all. False teachers can look impressive for a time. In the end their folly shows.

‘Disqualified’ is the opposite of the ‘approved’ workman of 2:15. Tested, they were found false.
passages.ot:
Exodus tells the story: “But Pharaoh called the wise men and sorcerers and magicians of Egypt, and they also did the same things by their magic arts” (Exodus 7:11). For a while they matched Moses. Then “Each one threw down his staff, and it became a serpent. But Aaron’s staff swallowed up the other staffs” (Exodus 7:12). Soon “The magicians tried to produce gnats using their magic arts, but they could not”, and they told Pharaoh, “This is the finger of God” (Exodus 8:18-19).

Jeremiah warned against teachers who spoke from their own minds: “They speak visions from their own minds, not from the mouth of the LORD” (Jeremiah 23:16). And Proverbs gives the reason to test what we hear: “The simple man believes every word, but the prudent man watches his steps” (Proverbs 14:15).
passages.hard:
Does verse 6 say that women are easily led astray?

No. Paul is describing particular women in Ephesus whom the false teachers had targeted, people weighed down with sin and caught in a cycle of endless learning that never reached the truth. He is not making a statement about women in general, and these verses must never be used to call women gullible or to keep them from learning. In his first letter to Timothy Paul insists that women must learn (1 Timothy 2:11). The same Timothy learned the Scriptures from his mother and grandmother (1:5; 3:15).

Notice where Paul's blame falls. It falls on the teachers who ‘worm their way into households’ and ‘captivate’ the vulnerable. Then as now, people who are carrying guilt or grief are easier for a manipulator to reach, men and women alike. Paul's words are a warning against those who prey on the weak, and a call to protect them.

If you have been harmed by a controlling leader or church, what was done was wrong, and it was not your fault. Being taken in by someone who seemed godly is not a sign of weak faith. You are free to step away and to tell someone you trust. If you were abused in other ways, or a crime was done, it should be reported to the authorities. A pastor or counsellor outside that church may help you sort out what happened. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Paul warns of teachers who slip into homes and prey on the weak. Ask whether there is anyone in your church who is carrying guilt or grief and is open to being misled, and how you could stand beside them. Ask whether you are always learning but never letting the truth change you. And ask whether you test what you hear, or believe every word.

passages.t: Paul's example; all who live godly lives will be persecuted
passages.happening:
Paul turns from the false teachers to Timothy. “You, however, have observed my teaching, my conduct, my purpose, my faith, my patience, my love, my perseverance, my persecutions, and the sufferings that came upon me in Antioch, Iconium, and Lystra. What persecutions I endured! Yet the Lord rescued me from all of them” (verses 10-11).

“Indeed, all who desire to live godly lives in Christ Jesus will be persecuted, while evil men and imposters go from bad to worse, deceiving and being deceived” (verses 12-13).
passages.hearers:
‘You, however.’ The false teachers had words and no life. Timothy had watched Paul's whole life up close: not only his teaching but his conduct, his aims, his faith and patience and love, and what all of it cost him.

Paul names three cities. On his first long missionary trip, in Pisidian Antioch, he and Barnabas were driven out of the district (Acts 13:50). In Iconium there was a plot to stone them (Acts 14:5). In Lystra, Timothy's own town, Paul was stoned and dragged out of the city, left for dead (Acts 14:19). Timothy may have seen some of this as a young man. It was there that he joined Paul soon afterward (Acts 16:1-3). He knew exactly what following Christ had cost his friend.

‘Yet the Lord rescued me from all of them.’ Paul does not mean he escaped all suffering. He was stoned. He means the Lord brought him through, and kept him for the work.

Then comes a hard sentence. ‘All who desire to live godly lives in Christ Jesus will be persecuted.’ Paul says this not as a threat but as a fact Timothy should expect. A world that resists Christ will resist those who follow him. It happened to Jesus first.
passages.ot:
The Old Testament is honest that God's people suffer for him: “Yet for Your sake we face death all day long; we are considered as sheep to be slaughtered” (Psalm 44:22). It is honest that God brings them through: “Many are the afflictions of the righteous, but the LORD delivers him from them all” (Psalm 34:19).

Jeremiah suffered for speaking God's word and could not keep silent: “His message becomes a fire burning in my heart, shut up in my bones” (Jeremiah 20:9). And Daniel's three friends, facing the furnace, said, “But even if He does not, let it be known to you, O king, that we will not serve your gods” (Daniel 3:18).
passages.hard:
‘All who desire to live godly lives in Christ Jesus will be persecuted.’ What does this mean, and what does it not mean?

It means that following Christ in a world that resists him will bring hard things, as it did for Jesus, for Paul, and for many believers through history. It does not say that suffering is good, or that it earns anything from God.

It also needs care. Paul was driven out of cities, stoned and chained. Being disagreed with, mocked online, or living among people who do not share your faith is not the same thing, and it is not wise to call every discomfort persecution. Nor is this verse a lesson for any party or side. Paul's answer to persecution was not to fight back or to seek power, but to keep loving, keep teaching and trust the Lord. Elsewhere he says, “Bless those who persecute you” (Romans 12:14).

And one more thing must be said. Not every hardship comes from following Jesus, and not every hardship is meant to be endured in silence. If you are carrying something heavy, whether persecution, illness, loss, or harm at the hands of others, it is right to seek help and safety. Please share it with someone you trust: a friend, a pastor, a counsellor. If you are in danger, or the pain ever feels like more than you can bear, reach out today to a crisis line or emergency service. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Timothy had watched Paul's whole life, not just his words. Ask who is watching yours, and what they are learning from it. Ask whether you have mistaken discomfort for persecution, or whether you have truly paid a price for following Christ. And ask how you would answer those who opposed you: with anger, or with blessing.

passages.t: Continue in the Scriptures: all Scripture is God-breathed
passages.happening:
“But as for you, continue in the things you have learned and firmly believed, since you know from whom you have learned them. From infancy you have known the Holy Scriptures, which are able to make you wise for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus” (verses 14-15).

“All Scripture is God-breathed and is useful for instruction, for conviction, for correction, and for training in righteousness, so that the man of God may be complete, fully equipped for every good work” (verses 16-17).
passages.hearers:
‘Since you know from whom you have learned them.’ Timothy learned the faith from people whose lives he had seen: his grandmother, his mother, and Paul. Truth came to him through people he could trust.

‘From infancy’ Timothy had known the Holy Scriptures. When Paul wrote, those were the Jewish Scriptures, what Christians now call the Old Testament. The New Testament had not yet been gathered, though Paul's letters were already being read in the churches. Paul says those Scriptures could make Timothy ‘wise for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus’. That is how the New Testament reads the Old: as a witness that leads to Jesus. Jesus himself said the Scriptures testify about him (John 5:39).

Then comes the word ‘God-breathed’. It is a rare Greek word, and this is one of its earliest known uses. It means breathed out by God. Scripture comes from God's own mouth, as the heavens did when God made them.

Paul then says what Scripture is for. It teaches what is true. It convicts, showing where we have gone wrong. It corrects, setting us right again. And it trains, like a coach, in a right way of living. The word for ‘fully equipped’ was used of fitting out a ship for a voyage, or giving a workman all his tools. Scripture gives God's servant what he needs ‘for every good work’.
passages.ot:
The psalms praise God's word in the same way. “The Law of the LORD is perfect, reviving the soul; the testimony of the LORD is trustworthy, making wise the simple” (Psalm 19:7). “the commandments of the LORD are radiant, giving light to the eyes” (Psalm 19:8). “Your word is a lamp to my feet and a light to my path” (Psalm 119:105).

God's word comes from his breath: “By the word of the LORD the heavens were made, and all the stars by the breath of His mouth” (Psalm 33:6). David said of his own words, “The Spirit of the LORD spoke through me; His word was on my tongue” (2 Samuel 23:2). And Moses told Israel that God's words “are not idle words to you, because they are your life” (Deuteronomy 32:47).
passages.hard:
What does ‘God-breathed’ mean for how Christians speak about the Bible?

Christians across the traditions confess together that Scripture comes from God and carries his authority. They also confess that it is fully human: its books show the words, style and lives of their writers. Very few Christians have ever thought the writers simply took dictation. God worked through their own minds, so that what they wrote was what he meant to say. As 2 Peter 1:21 puts it, “men spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit”.

Christians who share that confession describe it in different words. Many hold that Scripture is inerrant: because God cannot lie and Scripture is breathed out by him, it is without error in everything it affirms, including history and the world. Those who hold this do not demand wooden literal reading; they allow for round numbers, everyday speech such as ‘the sun rose’, loose quotation and the ways ancient writers wrote, and they apply the claim to what the writers first wrote. They argue that Jesus treated Scripture as unbreakable, and that a Bible which could err where it can be checked would give no firm ground where it cannot.

Others prefer to say Scripture is infallible: it never fails in what God gave it to do, to make people wise for salvation and to teach faith and life. They hold its authority just as fully. They point out that these very verses name the Bible's purpose, and they hold that some descriptions of nature and some details of history speak in the ordinary words and assumptions of the people God used, which they see as God stooping to human speech, not as a fault.

These differences are real, and they have divided schools and churches. But they are differences within a shared confession. These notes do not choose. The doctrine study ‘God Speaks: Revelation and Scripture’ sets out these views and others more fully.

Whatever words a Christian uses, Paul's point is the same: Scripture is given to be used, to make us wise for salvation in Christ and ready for good works.
passages.asks: Paul says Scripture can make you wise for salvation and equip you for every good work. Ask how much time you give to it, and whether you read it to be taught, corrected and trained, or only to find what you already think. Ask who taught you the Scriptures, and who you might help to know them. And ask what good work God might be equipping you for now.
